title.en: Why the Ant Is Not So Venomous as the Snake

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (tale recorded only here)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（此故事僅見於此地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 65 'Why the Ant is not so Venomous as the Snake', eBook #8299

summary.en: God first created the earth, then threw a rock from it onto the surface, breathing life into the fragments. The snake asks for the power to kill the rebellious, receives poison for its teeth; the ant, overjoyed at receiving the same privilege, runs off at such speed that it pays no attention when God calls — so God, enraged, takes away some of the ant's power, and the ant's bite is not so poisonous as the snake's. In a second Lipa telling, it is Bathala who slighted by a lazy ant transfers its intended gift to the snake and condemns ants to be pinched to death by those they bite.
summary.zh: 上帝造地後，又擲石碎塊、吹入生氣。蛇求誅惡之力，得齒中劇毒；螞蟻獲賜同權後狂喜奔走，上帝呼喚竟不應——上帝震怒，收回其部分之力。故今日蟻毒不及蛇毒。另一利帕傳說中，懶蟻怠慢巴哈拉，蛇得其原賜之能，蟻族則註定被其所咬者捏死。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator (Lipa, Batangas); archival record. Fansler notes a second local variant invoking Bathala; the tale is unrecorded outside Lipa.

passages.text: God first created the earth. Then he took a rock from the earth and threw it on the terrestrial surface; when the rock was broken into many small pieces, he breathed into them the breath of life, and they became living creatures. Among these creatures were the snake and the ant. One day the snake went to God to ask for power to kill all those that were rebellious and troublesome, and God answered, 'Hereafter you are endowed with the power to store in your teeth this poison. When you bite the vile and contemptible, inject into the wound some of this poison, and they will be killed; but first of all, observe their actions, and be conscientious and thoughtful.' The snake returned to the earth in great joy.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 65 'Why the Ant is not so Venomous as the Snake'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the ant heard that the snake was endowed with such power, it at once went to God to ask that the same privilege be granted it. 'Give me the same power, and I will be of great aid to the snake in destroying sinners,' it said; and God, thinking that the snake might need an assistant, gave the ant the same privilege that he had given the snake. The ant was so greatly overjoyed that it ran as fast as it could to the earth; when God saw it running he called to the ant, but it paid no attention to him. Then God, being very much enraged, took away some of the ant's power, lest the ant might use it unreasonably. And so to-day the ant's bite is not so poisonous as the snake's.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 65 'Why the Ant is not so Venomous as the Snake'; not verbatim.

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (with Bicol and Zambales variants)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（另有比科爾、三描禮士變體）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 66 'Why Locusts are Harmful', eBook #8299

summary.en: In the dawn of humanity angels headed by Satanas revolt against God; in battle Satanas throws a handful of sand into God's face, and God laughs — 'I turn the sand back to thee. The particles shall become the scourge of all ages to thee and to thy followers' — and the sand becomes a mighty swarm of locusts. Bicol and Zambales variants explain the pest instead from a greedy datu's exploding granaries and a goddess-beggar denied shelter by an ungrateful rich farmer.
summary.zh: 人類之晨，撒塔納斯率天使叛上帝；戰中撒沙入上帝之面。上帝大笑：『沙還於你——這些微粒將成為你與你的追隨者萬世之禍！』言畢沙粒化作鋪天蝗群。比科爾變體謂貪婪達圖糧倉爆裂、稻米化蟲；三描禮士變體謂富農拒施捨喬裝乞婦的財富女神，其稻穀化為蝗災。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. The notes' Bicol ('Origin of Locusts' from a hoarding datu) and Zambales (Kayamanan the goddess of riches disguised as a beggar) variants are paraphrased in the final passage as named variants.

passages.text: During the dawn of humanity, some angels headed by Satanas revolted against God; they wanted to establish a kingdom for themselves. In a battle against the army of God, in which God himself was present, Satanas threw a handful of sand into God's face; but the heavenly monarch just laughed, and said, 'I turn the sand back to thee. The particles shall become the scourge of all ages to thee and to thy followers, O Satanas!' No sooner had God uttered these words than the particles of sand became a mighty swarm of locusts that flew in all directions — such was the beginning of the pest.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 66 'Why Locusts are Harmful'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A Bicol variant explains the pest from greed: a valley datu hoarded his people's rice until, in a famine year, seven starving petitioners came begging and the datu, lunging at them from his ladder, fell and was left for dead; the next morning his bursting granaries exploded, and all the rice flew away in the form of insects — the doron — vanishing from his sight. In a Zambales variant an ambitious farmer, enriched by the goddess Kayamanan beyond six full barns, neglected his thank-feasts and drove away a beggar at whose plea he threatened to loose his dog; the beggar, who was the goddess in disguise, asked God for the power of changing anything to any form she wished, and doomed his rice to turn to a swarm of locusts which would destroy the crops of farmers everywhere — and the punishment was carried out, leaving the farmer destitute.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the variants printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 66 (Bicol by Maximina Navarro; Zambales by Felix de la Llana); not verbatim.

region.en: Laguna de Bay region, Luzon, Philippines (Paete and La Laguna versions)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖灣區（派提與內湖省版本）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 67 'How Lansones became Edible', eBook #8299

summary.en: Lansones fruit was once so poisonous its juice could bring leprosy. A starving religious pilgrim in the forest is fed the deadly fruit by an angel from heaven, and his hunger is removed — ever since, lansones have been good to eat, and all the fruits still bear the marks of the angel's fingers. In the Paete saint-legend, it is the Virgin Mary walking with her child who pinches the pulp with her white fingers, and the finger-prints of the Virgin may be seen in any lanzon opened today.
summary.zh: 昔日蘭撒果劇毒，汁液可致癩病。朝聖老者在林中飢疲交加，天使奉天而來，親手摘果餵之，飢餓頓消——自此蘭撒果甘美可食，果肉上至今留有天使指痕。派提鎮聖像傳說則謂聖母攜聖子親指甲果，開果可見聖母指印。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. Fansler notes the name-play lanson/lason ('poison') and the Paete Virgin-Mary legend (Benitez). Christianity-inflected etiology of a Malaysian fruit tree.

passages.text: Once upon a time the fruit of the lansone-tree was very poisonous; its very juice could make a man sick with leprosy. One day a very religious old man was passing through a forest to attend the fiesta of the neighboring town. When he reached the middle of the thick wood he became very hungry and tired, and felt that he could go no farther; no matter where he looked he could see nothing but the poisonous lansone-trees. So he lay down on the soft grass. Hardly a moment had passed when a winged being from heaven approached him and said, 'My good Christian pilgrim, take some of these lansone-fruits, eat them, and you will be much relieved.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 67 'How Lansones became Edible'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At first the old man would not do it, but the angel picked some of the fruits and handed them to the pilgrim. He then ate, and soon his hunger was removed; after thanking Heaven, he continued on his journey. Ever since this time, lansones have been good to eat, and all the fruits still bear the marks of the angel's fingers. In the Paete version, the missing image of the Virgin Mary was seen one evening walking over the grass with her child; when the thirsty child reached for the poisonous fruit, the mother took it from his hands and pinched the pulp gently with her delicate white fingers — 'Now you may take this and eat it. You will find it the most delicious and refreshing of all fruits' — and if any one discredits the story, he need only open any lanzon to see without fail the finger-prints of the Virgin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 67 and its notes (Paete version by Eulogio Benitez); not verbatim.

title.en: The Adam and Eve of the Tagalogs

region.en: Lubang, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's tale-source)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省盧邦（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral creation tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 67, 'The Adam and Eve of the Tagalogs', eBook #8299

summary.en: Bathala, envious that Laon the Visayan god had many subjects while his kingdom was a barren desert, asks Diwata the supreme god of the universe for aid; an angel brings seeds that clothe Luzon, and Bathala creates Adam and Eve, ancestors of the Tagalogs. Forbidden the green fruit of a certain plant, they disobey, are poisoned and made sick but not killed; they name the plant lason, implore forgiveness, and an angel marks each lason-seed with his finger-nails — after which the plant is renamed lanzon.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉見維薩揚神拉翁子民眾多，而己國荒蕪，遂求宇宙至高神迪瓦塔相助；天使攜種下凡，呂宋遍生草木。巴哈拉造亞當夏娃——他加祿人之祖。二人違禁偷食某植物青果，中毒病重而未死，遂名之曰『拉松』（毒）；悔罪得赦後，天使以指甲掐印果肉，去其毒性，植物改名『蘭松』。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog creation-fragment recorded by Fansler from Manuel Gallego's narration of a farmer's tale from Lubang, La Laguna; archival record. A Bathala-centered Eden parallel with the Eden-fall taboo motif; the first couple are not molded from clay but created by Bathala.

passages.text: Many hundreds of years ago, when Luzon was still uninhabited, Bathala, our supreme god, was envious of Laon, the god of the Visayans, because Laon had many subjects while Bathala's kingdom was a barren desert. It was within the power of Bathala to create human beings, but not food for them; and so he asked for advice from Diwata, the supreme god of the universe. Diwata told Bathala that the next day he would send an angel to earth with seeds to be planted; the promise was fulfilled, Bathala scattered the seeds all over Luzon, and within a short time the island was covered with trees and shrubs, ready for human habitation. Accordingly Bathala created Adam and Eve, the ancestors of the Tagalogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the variant printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 67, 'The Adam and Eve of the Tagalogs'; not verbatim.

passages.text: In spite of the fact that they were forbidden to eat the green fruit of a certain plant, they disobeyed and ate it; so, as a punishment, they were poisoned and made very sick — but they did not die. As a result of their experience, they gave the name lason ('poison') to this plant. Conscious of their fault, Adam and Eve implored forgiveness of Diwata; by order of Diwata, Bathala forgave the criminals, but the lason still remained poisonous. In order to rid it of its dangerous properties, an angel was sent to earth: he put the marks of his finger-nails on the surface of the pulp of each lason-seed, and these marks may be seen to this day. Afterwards the name of the plant was changed from lason to lanzon, the name by which it has been known ever since.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the variant printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 67, 'The Adam and Eve of the Tagalogs'; not verbatim.

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 68 'Why Cocks fight One Another', eBook #8299

summary.en: A childless king prays for an heir; an angel promises sons 'crowned with their own flesh.' Thirteen cocks are born to the royal family, each crowned at daybreak, but God forbids a cage of gold for them. When king and queen die, the feathered orphans, jealous of one another's crowns, begin fighting — and their descendants fight to this day.
summary.zh: 無嗣的國王祈求得子；天使允諾『其子將頭戴自身之肉為冠』。王室年年誕下一隻破曉即啼的公雞，共十三隻；上帝禁止為之造金籠。老王夫婦薨後，戴冠的孤雞互妒互鬥——其後裔相鬥至今。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. Explains cockfighting; Fansler knows no variants.

passages.text: Once upon a time in an unknown country there lived a royal couple endowed with almost all the blessings of God; their palace was decorated with precious stones, diamonds, sapphires, and emeralds, and celestial beings honored them with visits. Yet the king had a brooding melancholy: he had a happy and wealthy kingdom but no heir, nobody to manage the government after his death, and whenever the thought of death came to his mind he fell on his knees and implored the Almighty to give him a son.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 68 'Why Cocks fight One Another'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One evening an angel from Paradise came to visit him, and, finding the king at his prayers, said, 'Dry thy tears, O king! Thy royal prayer is heard in heaven. Thou shalt be given more than a son, but not in the same shape as thou art. Thy sons shall see the light of day crowned with their own flesh.' Not long afterward the queen gave birth to a cock that crowed on seeing the light of day, and every year a cock was born into the royal family until the feathered sons numbered thirteen; the couple would have made a cage of gold for them had not God forbidden it. But these sons were jealous of one another: each thought that the others had no right to wear crowns. At last the old king and queen died, and no one was left to manage the royal demesne but the dumb sons; thereafter the feathered orphans began fighting one another, each one trying to wrest the crown from the others.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 68 'Why Cocks fight One Another'; not verbatim.

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 69 'Why Bats fly at Night', eBook #8299

summary.en: The earth's single inhabitant, whose body was composed of warring minute organisms, lies dying on soft moss by a river; the organisms devour one another until only one survives, who flies away and becomes the ancestor of the bats. Daylight dazzles his eyes, so he flies only at night — and his descendants hide by day and come out only in the dark.
summary.zh: 大地唯有一人，身由相爭不息的微小生靈構成。他力竭倒臥河畔苔上；體內生靈互相吞食，最後僅存一個——它飛去，成為蝙蝠之祖。日光刺目，它只能夜飛；其子孫至今晝伏夜出。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. An odd cosmogonic fragment; Fansler knows no parallels.

passages.text: Many years ago the earth was inhabited by only one man. His body was composed of minute organisms that were incessantly warring against one another. One day this man became so weak that he could not obtain food for his support; he laid himself down on some soft moss by the bank of a river, and there he remained till night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 69 'Why Bats fly at Night'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The organisms that lived in his body began to fight against one another most fiercely. Each ate his fellow until he became very big. At last the man died, and only one organism remained alive. This organism then flew away, and became the ancestor of the bats. The light of day so dazzled his eyes that he could not fly very far, so he decided to fly only at night; and ever since, his descendants, too, have hidden themselves in the day-time, and come out only when it is dark.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 69 'Why Bats fly at Night'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Sun Shines More Brightly than the Moon

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 70 'Why the Sun shines more brightly than the Moon', eBook #8299

summary.en: The fairy's daughters Araw (kind) and Buwan (cruel) are each promised a universe-lighting diamond; God, descending as a beggar to test them, gives the diamond to Araw. Buwan steals one of God's diamonds from heaven, but hers proves less brilliant; two angels hurled into the sea both sisters, cast the two stones into the sky, and the bigger jewel was called Araw (sun), the smaller Buwan (moon).
summary.zh: 仙母二女：阿勞溫良、布婉乖戾。上帝備兩顆照徹宇宙的鑽石為姊妹之禮；他化身乞丐下凡察訪，把鑽石賜予善良的阿勞。布婉憤而竊取天上神鑽，卻不如姊姊的明亮；兩位天使將姊妹擲入海中，把雙石拋上天際——大者為日（Araw），小者為月（Buwan）。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. Sisters-as-luminaries with a morality test.

passages.text: Long, long ago there lived a fairy with two very beautiful daughters. Araw, the elder daughter, was very amiable and had a kindly disposition; but Buwan, unlike her sister, was disobedient, cruel, and harsh, always finding fault with Araw. One night, when the fairy came home from her nocturnal rambles and saw Buwan badly mistreating her elder sister, she asked God for help against her unruly daughter. Before this time God had prepared very valuable gifts for the two sisters — two enormous diamonds that could light the whole universe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 70 'Why the Sun shines more brightly than the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When God heard the prayer of the fairy, he descended to earth disguised as a beggar. On learning for himself how bad-tempered Buwan was, and how sweet and kind-hearted Araw, God gave the older sister her diamond as a reward. Buwan was greatly angered by this favoritism on the part of the Almighty: she went to the heavenly kingdom and stole one of God's diamonds, then returned to earth with the precious stone — but there she found that her jewel was not so brilliant as Araw's. When God went back to heaven and learned what Buwan had done, he sent two angels to punish her; but the angels abused their commission: they seized both sisters and hurled them into the sea. Then they threw the two stones upward into the sky, and there they stuck; but Araw's diamond was bigger and brighter than the one Buwan stole. Thereafter the bigger jewel was called Araw ('day' or 'sun'), and the smaller one, Buwan ('moon').
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 70 'Why the Sun shines more brightly than the Moon'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars (Pangasinan): Agueo and Bulan
title.zh: 日月星辰（邦阿西楠）：阿蓋歐與布蘭

region.en: San Carlos, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦阿西楠省聖卡洛斯（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pangasinan oral myth; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 70, 'The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars' (Pangasinan), eBook #8299

summary.en: Ama the father-god gives his favorite sons Agueo and Bulan fiery palaces that cross the earth side by side each day, lighting mankind together. Morose, obedient Agueo refuses the merry, mischief-loving Bulan's plea to hurry so thieves may work in darkness; the quarrel reaching their father's ears, he hurls an enormous rock at Bulan's palace — its shattered fragments, lit by contact with the fiery palace, are the stars — and Bulan is forbidden to travel with his brother, commanded instead to light the ways of thieves with his much-dimmed palace.
summary.zh: 父神阿瑪賜寵子阿蓋歐與布蘭各一座火宮，兄弟比肩日行，共照人間。沉默順從的阿蓋歐拒絕促行以便利盜賊，兄弟爭執傳至父神之耳；盛怒的阿瑪擲巨石擊中布蘭火宮——碎片沾火宮之光成為永恆的星辰——布蘭從此不得與兄同行，只許以其黯淡宮殿為盜賊引路。

sensitivity.note: Pangasinan myth recorded by Fansler from a Bulatao narrator; archival record. Brother-sun and moon-brother as rival palaces; the stars are the shattered rock.

passages.text: There was once a powerful god called Ama, 'father', the father and ruler of all others, and the creator of man. He had a wonderful aerial abode from which he could see everything. Of all his sons, Agueo ('sun, day') and Bulan ('moon') were his two favorites, and to these he gave each a fiery palace; in accordance with the wish of their father, Agueo and Bulan daily passed across the earth side by side, and together they furnished light to mankind. Agueo was of a morose and taciturn disposition, but he was always very obedient to his father; Bulan, on the other hand, was merry and full of mischief.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pangasinan myth printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 70, 'The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Once, when they were near the end of their day's labor, they saw thieves on the earth below, wishing that it were night so that they might proceed with their unlawful business. Bulan, who was one of their kind, urged Agueo to be quick, so that the earth might soon be left in darkness; as Agueo obstinately refused to be hurried, a quarrel ensued between the two brothers. Their father, who had been watching the two boys and had heard all that passed between them, became very angry with the mischievous Bulan, and in his wrath seized an enormous rock and hurled it whistling through the air. The rock struck the palace of Bulan and was broken into thousands of pieces, which got perpetual light from contact with the fiery palace; these may still be seen in the heavens, and they are called Bituen, 'stars'. Bulan was forbidden to travel with Agueo any more, but was commanded to light the ways of thieves henceforth with his much-dimmed fiery palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pangasinan myth printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 70, 'The Sun, the Moon, and the Stars'; not verbatim.

title.en: Apolaqui and Mayari: The Sun and Moon at War (Pampangan)
title.zh: 阿波拉奎與瑪雅莉：日月之戰（邦板牙）

region.en: Guagua, Pampanga, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋邦板牙省瓜瓜（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Pampangan oral myth; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), notes to Tale 70, 'The Sun and the Moon' (Pampangan), eBook #8299

summary.en: Bathala's children Apolaqui and Mayari are the first light of the earth from their eyes; when Bathala dies without a will, the brother refuses his sister any share in ruling, and the two fight with bamboo clubs until one of Mayari's eyes is put out. Stricken with pity, Apolaqui agrees they shall rule equally but at different times — Apolaqui the Sun rules the day with both eyes' light; Mayari the Moon rules the night, her light fainter, for she has but one eye.
summary.zh: 巴哈拉之子女阿波拉奎與瑪雅莉，目中之光為大地首光。巴哈拉猝逝無遺囑，兄長欲獨攬大權，兄妹以竹棍相鬥，瑪雅莉一目被打瞎。阿波拉奎愧悔，允諾分時而治——兄為太陽，晝以雙目之光照明；妹為月亮，夜半以獨眼微光照世。

sensitivity.note: Pampangan myth recorded by Fansler from a Layug narrator (Guagua); archival record. Fansler prints it with two Pampangan cradle-songs in which the Sun and Moon chase and duel; he judges these genuine old native tradition unmodified by Christianity.

passages.text: Long ago the earth was created and ruled by Bathala. He had two children, Apolaqui and Mayari. From the eyes of these two children the earth received its first light; the people, the birds of the air, the animals of the mountains, and even the fishes of the sea were glad because they had light, and so they were great friends of the two children. Bathala loved his children tenderly, and never wanted them to be separated from him: no matter how tired he was, he always followed them in their daily walks. But as time went on, and Bathala became old and feeble and could no longer keep up with his active son and daughter, he asked them to stay with him at all times; but they were so absorbed in their pleasures that they paid no heed to their father's wish.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pampangan myth printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 70, 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day he became sick, and died suddenly, without leaving any written will as to the disposition of his kingdom. Apolaqui wanted to rule the earth without giving any power to his sister Mayari; she refused to consent to her brother's plan, and a bitter conflict arose between them. For a long time they fought with bamboo clubs; at last Mayari had one of her eyes put out. When Apolaqui saw what he had done to his sister, he felt very sorry for her, and said that they should struggle no longer, but that they should exercise equal power on the earth, only at different times. Since that time, Apolaqui, who is now called the Sun, has ruled the earth during the day, and from his eyes we receive bright light; Mayari, who is called the Moon, rules the world at night — her light, however, is fainter than her brother's, for she has but one eye.
passages.note: Paraphrase of the Pampangan myth printed in Fansler's notes to Tale 70, 'The Sun and the Moon'; not verbatim.

title.en: Why the Culing Has a Tonsure

region.en: Lipa, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省利帕（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71a 'Why the Culing has a Tonsure', eBook #8299

summary.en: Taunted as lazy by the culing, the quail Pogô challenges him to see which can fly higher into the sky; the culing flies so high that his head touches the hot surface of the sky, and all the feathers on the top of his head are burned off — the culing's tonsure ever since.
summary.zh: 庫伶鳥譏鵪鶉懶惰；被激的鵪鶉反嗆『比比誰飛得更高』。庫伶一飛沖天，頭頂觸到灼熱的天幕，頭頂羽毛盡數燒落——庫伶自此『剃度』。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Africa narrator; archival record. Part of the southern-Luzon flight-contest group (with The Culeto and the Crow, The Hawk and the Coling).

passages.text: In a certain field there lived two birds, Pogô ('quail') and Culing, a small black bird that has no feathers on the top of its head. One day Pogô, while scratching the ground for food, met Culing, who said in a taunting tone, 'Where are you going, lazy one? Be more active. Don't be as lazy as a leech!' Pogô became very angry: 'You call me lazy! You are much lazier than I. Let us see which can fly higher into the sky!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71 'Why the Culing has a Tonsure'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Thereupon Culing agreed, and he began to fly upward until he was lost from sight. He flew so high that his head touched the surface of the sky; as the sky was hot, all the feathers on the top of his head were burned off, and ever since, the culing has had a tonsure.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71 'Why the Culing has a Tonsure'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Culeto and the Crow: The Race to the Sky's Door
title.zh: 小黑鳥與烏鴉：天門之賽

region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71b 'The Culeto and the Crow', eBook #8299

summary.en: Shortly after the Deluge, the white-feathered crow mocks the tiny culeto; nettled, the culeto proposes a race, 'One, two, three!' — separated by a dense cloud, the culeto flies at full speed and knocks his head very hard against the door of the sky, scraping a large piece of skin from his scalp, while the crow, having lost his way, flies so near the sun that his feathers are burned black. The bald culeto and the black crow descend from that single bet.
summary.zh: 洪水方退，白羽烏鴉譏笑小黑鳥庫勒托；庫勒托憤而提議競飛。一聲令下，二鳥直上雲霄——密雲隔開兩者；庫勒托全速衝天，頭撞天門、頭皮揭去一大片；迷路的烏鴉飛近太陽，白羽燒成烏黑。一場賭賽，留下禿頂小鳥與黑鴉。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. A favorite among Tagalog children, told by old men at barber-shops.

passages.text: Once upon a time, shortly after the Deluge, the crow was merrily crowing on the branch of a tree when the culeto came by. The crow's voice was so harsh that the culeto made fun of it: 'Good-morning, Mr. Crow! I am very glad to hear you sing. Your voice is so fine, that I cannot help closing my ears.' 'Pray, think first of yourself!' answered the crow. 'What do I care for a good voice, so long as I have a strong body? Why don't you laugh at yourself? See how weak and tiny you are!' 'Weak!' said the culeto. 'Do you call me weak? I would fly a race even with an eagle.' 'The idea of racing the eagle when you do not even dare race me!' laughed the crow. 'The strength of a person is not to be judged by his size. Don't you know that it is the smallest pepper that is the hottest?'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71 'The Culeto and the Crow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Well, then, if you wish to race me now at your own risk, let us begin!' replied the crow. 'One, two, three!' counted the culeto, and up they flew. During their flight the two birds became separated from each other by a dense cloud. The culeto flew at full speed so high upward that he knocked his head very hard against the door of the sky — so hard, in fact, that a large piece of skin was scraped from his scalp. The crow, having lost his way, flew so near the sun that his feathers were burned black. It is on account of this bet between the culeto and the crow that all the descendants of the former have been bald-headed, while all the descendants of the crow have black feathers to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71 'The Culeto and the Crow'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Hawk and the Coling: The Salt That Melted

region.en: Taal, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (story well known in every town there)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省塔阿爾（故事聞名全鎮）

texts.period: Tagalog oral etiological tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71c 'The Hawk and the Coling', eBook #8299

summary.en: A hawk challenges the little coling to a loaded race: the hawk carries cotton, the coling salt. Rain soaks and weighs the cotton while the salt dissolves away, and the coling overtakes the hawk, flying so high his head touches the sun. The hawk claims victory, saying the coling fell dead — but the coling returns and shows the bald top of his head as proof, and the crow-judge awards him the race.
summary.zh: 鷹向小黑鳥科林提出負重競飛：鷹負棉花，科林負鹽。驟雨浸透棉花愈飛愈重，鹽卻溶化無蹤；科林反超，直上觸日，頂羽盡焦。鷹落地謊稱科林已摔死；科林歸來，以禿頂為證——烏鴉裁判判其獲勝。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog etiological tale recorded by Fansler from a Gaa narrator (Taal); archival record. Third form of the southern-Luzon flight-contest group; Fansler compares a Ceylon tale of the crow and drongo.

passages.text: Early one morning a hawk sallied forth from his nest to find something to eat, flying so high that he could hardly be seen from the earth; descending, he saw a coling sitting quietly on a branch, despised the little bird, and challenged him to a flight upward. The coling asked to have it the next morning before sunrise, and added, 'Each of us is to carry a load with him to make the flight a little more difficult.' 'I will take some salt,' said the coling; 'Then I will take some cotton,' replied the hawk — the coling went to the sea for salt, the hawk to the cotton-field, and the crow who was present agreed to judge the contest, giving a caw as the starting signal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71 'The Hawk and the Coling'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At first the hawk flew faster and higher than the coling; but very soon it began to rain. The cotton on the hawk's back became soaked with water and soon was very heavy; but the salt on the coling's back was soon dissolved, and then he had no load at all. Under these conditions the coling soon overtook the bigger bird, and in a little while longer the hawk could no longer see his rival — but the coling flew so high that at last his head touched the sun, and all the feathers on the top were burned off. The hawk flew down to the crow and said that he had won the race, for the coling had fallen to the ground dead; but by and by the coling himself came, and showed them the top of his head as proof that he had won. The crow gave his decision in favor of the coling, and the hawk flew off disgraced — and from that time all colings have had the tops of their heads bald, to show that they are the descendants of the victorious bird.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 71 'The Hawk and the Coling'; not verbatim.
